speechtext: That the third report of the special committee appointed to inquire into agricultural conditions be concurred in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
This report, which was read yesterday or the day before, calls for the appointment by the government of a royal commission to inquire into the grain trade, and adds a recommendation that this com-

Agricultural Conditions
mission be given powers by the federal authorities and also by the provincial legislatures. I have grave doubts as to the wisdom of the latter proviso. Some of the legislatures concerned, perhaps all three of them, are sitting. But, in the light of the decision of the Court of Appeal of Manitoba regarding the powers of the commission which was appointed by the late government and which was arrested in its work, I am not clear as to what powers which this government is not amply authorized to confer the committee desires to place in this commission. I do not know what the provincial powers are that the committee has in mind. It seems to me that the proviso is going to delay the work of the commission, a commission which, it will be recalled, I urged to be appointed in my . speech on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. What is the need of that proviso? Would it not be better to eliminate it and appoint a strong commission amply armed with federal powers-for our powers of investigation are very wide indeed-rather than put in the way of the commission impediments that may result not only in delay but possibly in disaster?
Mr. Speaker-
The hon. member has exhausted his right to speak. Perhaps the seconder of the motion might deal with the subject.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
There is no trade in Canada that has been so often investigated as the grain trade. I have before me a record showing that between 1897 and 1921, a period of twenty-four years, there were fourteen royal commissions, federal and provincial. In 1921, a royal commission was appointed to investigate the trade, and it is within the memory,
I imagine, of almost every member of the House that the work of that commission was blocked through an injunction obtained in the courts. I have no legal knowledge nor any legal pretensions, but my recollection is that the action to obtain that injunction upon the commission was taken under provincial statute. With the wish therefore to avoid the possibility of a recurrence of such an injunction, I take it, the committee on Agricultural Conditions unanimously put in this proviso. The government have no pronouncement to make on the issue raised by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). If it is the desire of parliament that there should be another investigation into the grain trade the government are quite willing to carry out that desire, and it will necessi-fMr. Meighen.]
tate the placing of an amount in the Supplementary Estimates. If, however, in the judgment of legal men the proviso will delay the proceedings, then, of course, it might be a matter for conference, and I am not sure whether my hon. friend who is chairman of the special committee (Mr. McMaster) would not desire to look n ore carefully into that aspect of the subject. But I would appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, that the chairman of the committee, who has no doubt given the matter legal consideration, and possibly has already consulted with the Justice department, might be unanimously given the right to explain the legal features of the matter.
Without precluding other members from speaking.

With the unanimous consent of the House the hon. chairman of the committee may, of course, speak again. I may say to other hon. members, however, that when the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) speaks he will close the debate, and if any hon. member desires to speak on the subject he should do so now.

I think I have already placed myself on record during this session in regard to this matter. Speaking, as I have previously said, in behalf of the producers, I believe that they should have the privileges which a commission of this kind would afford. While it is true, as the minister states, that fourteen commissions have been appointed within a certain number of years to investigate the grain trade, it does seem to me that events have shown in the past that the producers, the men who have the real grievances, have not had an opportunity of placing their views before any commission. At all events, the results have never been to their satisfaction. I have many letters in my office to-day from individuals throughout the country who endorse the attitude I have taken in the past on this subject, when I have urged the appointment of a commission specifically for the purpose of hearing what the producers have to say. And I have tried to point out that in all parliamentary committees appointed by the government such expert evidence as has been given has resulted, I honestly believe, detrimentally to the interests of the producers. My only plea for a commission is based on the desire to facilitate the producers in laying their case before such a body.

Let me say in the first instance that if we can do anything to facilitate a proper inquiry into

Agricultural Conditions
the grain trade we want to do it; and I may add that our attitude is exactly the same as it was in 1921. The only thing we are afraid of, however, is that, very likely unwittingly, nay, I will go further and say, absolutely unwittingly, because I know the hon. chairman of the committee-there is a grave danger of our going through the same sort of farce that we went through last year in connection with the wheat board. It is a great deal better to do something we know we can do ourselves than to undertake anything in regard to which our powers are open to dispute. We know at the present time that we can make a certain investigation, and possibly having regard to all the different matters which will be found to be a proper subject of inquiry we might be able to legislate as broadly and as fully as we should like to. I admit that what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) says is technically correct, there have been many different investigations; but I think he will look in vain for any general investigation into this business in the last ten years. He will not find one. I should like to have the minister converted to the idea of the great necessity of a proper investigation.
I admit it.

We tried to convert him last session, and I thought we had succeeded. Indeed, I thought we had a pledge from him that there was going to be an investigation during the recess. We gave him a vote of $50,000, I think, for that purpose, and apparently all parties wanted the investigation.
Now, in so far as the strict legal position is concerned, it is perfectly true, as the hon. minister has pointed out, that interests which did not want the investigation that was being conducted by the Grain Inquiry Commission applied for an injunction and stopped the investigation temporarily. That injunction ought never to have been issued according to the unanimous opinion of the Court of Appeal of the province of Manitoba, which, reversing the decision of the trial judge, held that this parliament had absolute power to order the investigation. We thought the investigation should have been resumed, but we did not have control of the matter and nothing further was done.
Our only desire, Mr. Speaker, is to have a real investigation as quickly and fully as such an investigation can properly be held, so that we may know eixactly what the troubles are, if troubles there be. And certainly we have heard of many; why, every
day we are receiving complaints. Cannot we find out what the truth is and remove grievances which, I have no doubt, exist? We want to help our hon. friends, and we know we are helping them for we told them to go ahead and not get themselves in a position where possibly they would be held up through misunderstandings or by obstacles raised here and there. Surely, for the present at any rate, the unanimous judgment of the Court of Appeal of Manitoba, unappealed as it has been, ought to be enough for us.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the confusion that has arisen in regard to this report is possibly the result of its wording. If I understand the purpose the committee has in mind, it is that this government should appoint a royal commission, and that if any of the provincial governments desire to cooperate they themselves should give powers to that particular commission. In other words, it is to permit the same gentlemen to exercise all the authority that can come to them from both the federal and provincial governments. If that is correct, I would say that so far as our government is concerned we will endeavour promptly to appoint a commission and to have in mind, in the selection of its personnel,, the choice of gentlemen who would inspire the confidence of the governments that are likely to unite to cooperate in this matter. If that is the view of the committee it ought to settle the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a member of the committee on Agricultural Conditions, but I have some knowledge of the legal position, and particularly of the injunction which the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has referred to. An injunction was taken out and supported by the trial judge, who held that the commission was improperly issued and was beyond the powers of the Dominion authorities. As my right hon. friend has said, there was an appeal from that decision, and the Court of Appeal reversed the trial judge's finding, holding that the Dominion authorities had power to create that commission. The point in argument in support of the injunction was that the commission covered matters which were not within the purview of the Dominion parliament, but were solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. That argument was not supported by the Court of Appeal. But since this decision of the Court of Appeal the Privy Council has decided that the act which
Agricultural Conditions

created the Board of Commerce was ultra vires. That had a direct bearing on the extent of the Dominion's powers in regard to matters such as this, and following that decision the Manitoba Court of Appeal held that some portions at least af the Canada Grain Act were ultra vires of the Dominion. For that reason if a commission is now issued solely under Dominion authority questions may be raised which were raised in the preceding case, and may create obstacles.

I thank you Mr. Speaker, and the House for giving me an opportunity to briefly address hon. members in connection with the report which was brought in unanimously by the committee of which I have the honour to be chairman. When we had the matter of investigating the grain trade brought before us we first of all discussed whether or not we should make the investigation ourselves. We came to the conclusion that if we attempted such an investigation we should have to set aside for the time being all our other work; it would give us more than really we could accomplish ourselves. Then I was asked to confer with the law officers of the Crown to see whether there was some way of obviating the situation which arose in connection with the last royal commission which was stopped in the course of its investigation by a judgment of the court of first instance in Manitoba. True, that judgment was set aside by the higher court of that province, but in rendering judgment the Court of Appeal indicated that, although a royal commission appointed by the federal power had the right to make a general investigation, still in the course of that investigation questions might come up touching contract, property and civil rights which would fall under provincial jurisdiction, and which might lay the investigation proposed to be carried on by the commission open to attack by any one who came before the provincial courts. So we proposed that the government should appoint a commission and should invite the provinces to name the same gentlemen as commissioners for the same purpose, and that these gentlemen should start their work clothed with every power that the sovereign authority of the provinces interested or the sovereign authority of the Dominion might bestow upon them. It seemed to me that that was a wise proceeding to take. It may consume a little more time at the beginning but certainly it opens a way for a full and complete investigation without possibility of let or hindrance.
Motion agreed to.
On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), only he is not present, if he would give orders to expedite bringing down the report of the commissioners who investigated the wreck of the Alaskan off the coast of British Columbia. This wreck investigation took place on the second of February; the investigation commission sat then, and on one or two subsequent days. This is the sixteenth of March, and I think the report might be forthcoming by this time.
On the Orders of the Day:

On the 12th of this month, an order was passed calling for production of the correspondence with the British government relating to the Halibut Fisheries Treaty and the execution thereof. Of course, that is four days ago. Some orders might take pretty long in preparation; but this concerns only one department. The correspondence would not likely be very long, and I think an hour would likely be enough in which to copy it. I was expecting the return yesterday or to-day.

speechtext: I think I can promise to give my right hon. friend most of the papers to-day. The delay has been on account of a cable having been sent to the British government to ask a question with respect to some of the papers, and the reply not yet having been received.

maintopic: PROPOSED CUSTOMS OFFICER AT NEW YORK
speechtext:
A despatch has come from British Columbia dealing with the question of a customs officer at New York. It quotes Mr. Oliver, the Premier of British Columbia, as saying that:
-when he drew the attention of Premier King and Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance, to the fact that duty was being collected on goods going from eastern Canada to British Columbia, they were astounded. The existing customs regulations laid it down that Canadian goods transhipped in a foreign port, unless under supervision of a Canadian customs officer, bad to pay duty on entry into Canada. Yet, when British Columbia asked for the establishment in New York of a customs officer, the application was refused.
I want to ask if, in fact, the government have refused the application for a customs officer at New York. Because, I should like to say, this is a question in which public bodies, boards of trade and so on, at the coast, are greatly interested, and I understood the government had the matter still under consideration, and perhaps favourable consideration. This is a statement by the Premier of British Columbia.

maintopic: PROPOSED CUSTOMS OFFICER AT NEW YORK
speechtext: Does the hon. member want the Prime Minister to answer?

maintopic: PROPOSED CUSTOMS OFFICER AT NEW YORK

maintopic: PROPOSED CUSTOMS OFFICER AT NEW YORK
speechtext: An application has been made to place a customs officer at New York to look after the traffiic that goes via the ocean and the Panama canal. This matter has been under the consideration of the department, and while the department has not decided definitely, it feels inclined to refuse the application, because this would divert traffic towards the United States and all the Canadian railways would get out of it would be the haul from the-point of departure to the boundary-the whole of the railroad haul to the sea and the whole of the ocean freight would go to the United States.
On the Orders of the Day:

I notice that in the estimates provision has been made for the appointment of commissioners to visit South America and Great Britain with a view to securing trade in Canadian pure-bred stock. When will the report be placed on the Table or has it already been placed on the Table?
I have one of the reports ready. The other one will be ready, I expect, in the course of a day or two.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair:
Immigration-outside service-salaries, $700,000.
Mr.- HOEY: It was not my intention to take part in this discussion which has already become unduly long. I feel, however, that I should refer to the address delivered during the course of this debate by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I regret that that hon. member felt it incumbent upon him to make certain statements, not because I believe the statements were in themselves untrue. In so far as they relate to Alberta, they may be conservative, but in so far as they relate to western Canada, as I know it, they are hopelessly and outlandishly exaggerated. The weakness of his address, it seems to me, lay in the fact that he failed to distinguish between conditions for which a mistaken economic policy has been responsible and conditions that are inherent in or natural to the territory which he described. Naturally our sympathies all go out to hon. members who have come from other lands, lands of peace and prosperity, and we can all realize their anxiety to return and enjoy the peace and prosperity associated in our minds with those lands from which they originally came.
I want to follow very closely in one particular the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. MacLaren), when he decided to discuss this problem of immigration from a purely sectional standpoint. I want to look at it from the standpoint of the province of Manitoba, with which I am most familiar, and in doing that I want to answer the question put, I think, by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell), the chief interrogator for the Liberal party, who.asked. "Why should we bring immigrants into this country?"
Supply-Immigration

Turning to the province of Manitoba for a moment, what do we find? We find in that province political, educational, religious and social institutions far in excess of our present needs. We have in the province of Manitoba a parliament building of which we are justly proud, that was built in all good faith anticipating immigration, a structure which cost almost exactly as much as this edifice in which I speak this afternoon. We have also in that province an agricultural college, one of the finest in the Dominion of Canada, an agricultural college that cost us millions of dollars and costs us now hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to maintain an institution the capacity of which has never been tested. Nor is that all. If we turn eastward from Winnipeg to the Winnipeg river, we find there a complete power plant. It was opened in January of this year at a cost of exactly $6,000,000, money invested largely by American investors, business men of astuteness, men who have unshakable faith in the future of that province-an electrical plant that is at present giving us electricity far in excess of our present needs, the cheapest light and power on the American continent, a plant that ought ultimately to make the city of Winnipeg one of the largest industrial centres on the American continent.
If we turn to lake Winnipeg we have there in our fisheries, if they are carefully guarded and legitimately exploited, a source of inexhaustible wealth. We have our mining areas in the north, two of which have just recently been opened up, the value of which has not yet been determined. I say that the institutions to which I have referred earlier in my remarks were all built, in my judgment, in good faith. But we are over-institutionalized. I am not blaming anybody in the province of Manitoba to-day for that, but we are groaning and staggering under the burden of taxation resulting therefrom.
Let me take hon. members in imagination just for a moment or two to a typical Manitoba town. The train service is tri-weekly. We arrive at the depot and get into conversation with the station agent. If he is an honest man-and all station agents are honest men, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) well knows-what will he tell us? He will tell us what hundreds of- them have told me, that they could handle three times the traffic that they are at present handling, and handle it just as efficiently without one cent of added cost to the company. Turning to the section men what do we find?	Exactly
the same conditions. Go into the village itself and there you will find two' or three storekeepers who are unemployed FMr. Hoey.]
two-thirds of their time. Go into the schools immediately adjoining that territory, and what do you find? You find school teachers, employed at a salary of approximately $100 per month, teaching seven, ten or fifteen youngsters, when they could just as efficiently teach forty-five. We find in those territories -and I know Manitoba; I do not take second place to any member in this House in my knowledge of Manitoba and conditions in that province; I stand open to correction, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) sits to my left-we find in those territories men attempting to farm-shall I say, or to scratch? -large areas of land. In this regard I often think of a story I once heard of a farm wife who sent a youngster out to set the hen on some eggs. She gave him a specified number, and when he returned she asked him how he accomplished the task. He said, "I accomplished it fine. I set the hen down on two hundred eggs." "Oh", she said in astonishment, "a hen can never cover two hundred eggs." "I know that", the boy replied, "but I did it just to see the old fool trying to spread herself." It. is most pitiful, Mr. Chairman, to see the attempts on the part of certain sincere but mistaken agriculturists in the province to "spread themselves". Almost everything has been sacrificed-in some cases the education of their children, domestic utensils in the home, all sacrificed-in a mad lust to acquire more land. What would immigration mean to these districts? It would mean, first of all, a daily train service, and a daily train service would mean a daily postal service. It would mean the enrichment of the social life and the satisfaction of the social instincts of that community. It would add no extra burden so far as the maintainance of the institutions is concerned. That is my point.
I pass from that to what I consider to be the cardinal fallacy that has entered into this debate. "If you bring settlers into Canada you are going to increase production, and increased production will mean deflation of prices, if indeed you can obtain a market for your products at all." It is scarcely necessary to deal with such a fallacy; it is so pitifully obvious. If you bring an agriculturist from the United States and establish him in the province of Manitoba, does he still remain a producer in the United States? If you bring an immigrant from southern or northern Europe, or even from Ireland, does he remain a producer in Ireland? You cannot cut out competition by shutting men out of the country. The crux of the whole question is, are we going to bring them in

Supply-Immigration
here to co-operate with us or let them remain outside to compete with us? That is the crux of the whole situation. "Oh," you say, "if you keep out European industrial workers we exclude competition and keep up the price of wages." Do you? You cannot keep out their products except by the erection of tariff barriers in which my hon. friends do not believe. Personally I cannot follow a course of reasoning that would allow manufactured articles to come in, and deny men the right to enter this country and manufacture such articles here. That is the cardinal point. "But", you say, "we can keep them in Europe; it is true we cannot keep them from competing with us, if they are Slavs, on the free markets of England, but we can keep them unemployed in Europe." Yes, but to the extent that you keep them unemployed there you paralyze Europe's purchasing power, and consequently cause reaction against your own trade and commerce.
I want to make this suggestion to the minister, with whom I have considerable sympathy and in whose sincerity I absolutely believe, I want to ask him if he has ever seriously considered the advisability of extending to rural areas in this province the housing scheme created by the late government and confined until now to the urban centres. We might establish in the province of Manitoba-or indeed, for that matter, anywhere in Canada-a standard farm labourer's dwelling constructed out of concrete, indestructible, at a cost of say $2,500; we might establish such cottages on our larger tracts of land, give the farm labourer a home in which to live with an acre of land upon which he could produce during the summer months sufficient to keep him and his family during the winter, a little cottage where his wife could board the hired help of the farmer that are now a nuisance-I might precede that by an adjective but I do not want to-to the over-worked farmer's wife, where the wife of the farm labourer could help the farmer's wife during the busjr season of the year, and where the farm labourer's family could grow un and enjoy the great advantages of rural life. Similar homes have been erected in European countries, the suggestion is in no sense original. After you had erected such homes and had brought men with their families and established them there, after they had acquired experience and had become familiar with Canadian conditions, is it not the most likely thing in the world that the man who is to-day farming two sections would enter into an agreement with his farm labourer now Canadianized

I mean Canadianized in so far as farming experience is concerned-to take over half of the land he is attempting to scratch.
Reference has been made by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), to unemployment in the city of Winnipeg. Unemployment exists .there. Unemployment has always existed in Winnipeg, and personally I do not think the government treated Winnipeg fairly in regard to unemployment relief this year. Winnipeg has for years been the rendezvous for the surplus farm labour of the three prairie provinces. You can talk to thousands of them on the train, and what do they tell you? "We are going to the Peg. there's no other burg on the prairies big enough to give us a good time." The result is that they crowd in from bankrupt Alberta and from comparatively prosperous Saskatchewan, causing unemployment, causing congestion, creating chaos-and the city of Winnipeg has got to maintain them. We have a real grievance, speaking as an industrial worker in the city of Winnipeg, against the agriculturists of the prairies; and I think the time has come when we have a right to demand of them that they absorb their surplus farm help in the fall of each year. How can they expect us to maintain it?

Does my hon. friend not
believe in immigration? If so, why does he object to this labour immigrating to Winnipeg?	[DOT]
Mr. HOEY; I say the time has come when we have a right to demand that these agriculturists, a great many of whom are in no sense insolvent, absorb their own surplus labour. And I want to say that after fifteen years' intensive study of the rural problem in the province of Manitoba, I do not think this labour can ever hope to become absorbed until some such scheme as I have indicated is launched. Personally I would take the whole amount to be voted for immigration this year and build farm labour cottages. The building of these cottages would cause employment and stimulate the building trades; it would distribute wealth in this country and go far to create a spirit of optimism; and when you have these homes constructed I can assure you that there are thousands with their families to-day in the urban centres who will be glad to go out and take possession of them. The scheme may seem impracticable, it did seem so to me at one time, but it is the best suggestion I can submit.
I am opposed to the co-operation of the government with the Canadian Colonization Association-not because I know anything of
Supply-Immigration

that body, but because I believe the co-operation does no go far enough to achieve practical results. But it goes far enough to create suspicion in the minds of the people, and create a great deal of unpopularity so far as the government is concerned. That, without knowing anything about the association, is the position that I take. If I were the minister I would put forth a supreme effort to interest the provincial departments of immigration. I would propose to the province of Manitoba that their department of immigration, which has been dead for some years, might be resuscitated and placed under the Minister of Agriculture, the federal government perhaps, paying the salary of the Deputy Minister of Immigration. I would propose some such policy to all of the provincial governments. I would go further than that, I would get in touch with our municipal reeves, and our municipal councils throughout the province; I think that the thing might be very profitably discussed if we are going to have a conference on the problem of taxation in this country. And then I would utilize the whole machinery associated with the Soldier Settlement Board. Now, if the federal government, the provincial governments, the municipal authorities and the Soldier Settlement Board cannot put across this scheme of immigration I do not think the Canadian Colonization Association can. The co-operation which is proposed by the minister is going to be interpreted as a tacit confession of failure on the part of the Dominion government to undertake a task which is paramountly their duty.
Now, just a word with regard to the type of immigrant that should come in. I have come in contact with thousands of so-called non-English-speaking people in the province of Manitoba. I have entered their homes; I have met them in a thousand and one different ways. I want to say that they are not the most prosperous people in the province to-day, but they are as prosperous as other sections of our Manitoba people and, I think, the most contented. They were driven up into the northern sections of the province; they had to encounter almost unsurmountable obstacles. They have made good, their young men are entering the universities and graduating with honours; they are entering the professions; they are a source of pride not only to Manitoba but to the Dominion as a whole. But when you turn to the class of immigrants that we should encourage to come in, it is a somewhat difficult task to determine the most desirable type. Personally I am opposed to bringing into

this country any man who has passed the age of 35 years. You can never detach him from the old country habits and from the old country methods of doing things. Again and again he will remind you of the kind of trains they have in the Old Country, the way they live there and the way they do things there. If you bring him out when he is comparatively young, he forgets the Old Country. I never think of the Old Country. Therefore, I would discourage men who are past the age of 35 years coming to this country.
Speaking of Scandinavians I would admit all the Scandinavians into Canada to-morrow and would be prepared to accept the responsibility for so doing. I never met in western Canada a Scandinavian who was, if you will pardon the colloquialism, " broke." I remember a former American school teacher in Minnesota paying me a great tribute on one occasion when I was in conversation with her. She asked me how long I had been in that part of the country where I resided.
I said I had been there three years. She said " How did you acquire such a working knowledge of English?" I said they spoke English in the land from which I came. She . said "Have you not come from Sweden?" The Scandinavians are the best settlers that have been brought to this country. But when you are deciding the type of settlers it all depends on the ambition of the individual, and unfortunately it is difficult to detect ambition in a man-when you are first introduced to him it is absolutely impossible.
I can remember an immigrant who came to this country some fourteen years ago. When he arrived in the city of Quebec he had not $35 which, at that time, it was necessary for him to have in order to land. But by his ingenuity he evaded the immigration authorities and got in. He came up to the city of Montreal, and unemployment at that time was rampant. After two hours' search he secured a job in a Montreal tannery owned by a Scotchman, washing and stretching hides. The old employer said to him " The work is difficult and onerous, but the wages are high ", and he received for his work in that tannery for two months $7 a week. He saved in that two months enough money to take him to Fort Frances in New Ontario, where he obtained a position at $400 a year, where he worked for two years and saved enough to enable him to take a five-year college course-that is, with the little additional sums the he was able to earn during the college vacation. We sometimes hear of men living on a meal a day. This particular immigrant

Supply-Immigration
lived for four days on one meal, and I remember on one occasion he lived for five days on one meal, and the last six weeks of the year in which he graduated he lived for ten cents a day, and was denied
4 p.m. the privilege of writing home to his [DOT]	parentte, because he did not have the
money for postage. His parents were then living but have since died. He graduated from that institution, and is to-day a member of the Dominion parliament. He is still in his thirties, and by no means a physical wreck. I wish to say that even the discussions that have taken place on this subject have not shaken my faith in the Dominion of Canada. With that experience, Mr. Chairman, could I honestly and conscientiously deny young ambitious men the right to come into this country? I would not encourage them to come in, and I would not spend a cent to bring them in, but I would allow them to come if they so desired. We have a tremendous debt in this country. We have social conditions that are depressing, but I believe we can bring immigrants in here who will help us surmount these difficulties, and help us pay off these financial obligations, and in the meantime these immigrants may enjoy a measure of prosperity which is greater than you can enjoy in any other country in modem civilization.

I find myself, Mr. Chairman, very much in agreement with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) and I think it entirely proper that I should congratulate him upon the attitude he takes on this question. I certainly agree with him in his statement that immigration in this country is a great necessity. I look upon the problem of immigration as the greatest problem facing this country to-day. It is the country's most important business and likewise the most important business of this House. Canada cannot develop without an increase in her population. The subject of immigration cannot be considered except in relation to three things, farm industry, our railways and our industrial concerns. Each one of those has its own bearing upon this subject. Our farmers complain that they are not making profits today. I think .the same is true of our industrials. Canada is over-industrialized, she is over-built with railways, and at the present time all classes are suffering owing to the lack of markets. The hon. member for Springfield said: Are we going to bring in immigrants to co-operate with . us, or leave them out to compete with us? I think that is all very well, so far as it goes,
but if they co-operate with us they will certainly create markets for our farmers and for our manufacturers, and traffic for our railways, and increased traffic will produce what the farmers so urgently desire, lower freight rates, and thereby lessen the cost of their agricultural implements and other necessities. Increased production and increased markets must also enable the manufacturer to reduce his overhead, and by increasing the volume of his production, enable him to reduce the price at which it can be sold. Furthermore this increase in population will mean , more people to share our burdens of taxation.
A great deal has been said with regard to the question of emigration. I believe that emigration from our farming community has resulted from the burdens borne by these farmers due to high freight rates, due to the fact that they are not getting more for their produce, or very little more, than they were before the war, and due to the decreased value of our dollar. Therefore, our farmers are leaving, wherever they can, for better farms, or better places to earn a living. The lack of markets has caused stagnation in industries and building trades. The result is that our skilled artisans, our professional men, our architects are leaving the country to go to the United States where there is an industrial boom. But when we create those conditions which are bound to result from an increased population these men will flow back into the country.
I believe that the matter of great importance in connection with any policy of immigration is to select immigrants from the right sort of people, and the qualifications of such people, in my opinion, are these. First, the mental capacity of the immigrants; secondly, I would see to it that we secure people whom we can assimilate; and thirdly, I would insist that the people who come are such as will not drag down the standard of living in Canada. We in British Columbia have a very good illustration of the sort of immigrants we cannot assimilate, in the orientals who have been allowed to come into the country. And the people in the East, I believe, have also had an example of people whom it is impossible to absorb into the populatitjn in those immigrants who go into the city of Montreal, for instance, and work in the sweat shops, thus driving out our best labour from the manufacturing industries and forcing them to seek employment elsewhere. I know of two industrial concerns in Hamilton, one of which has failed recently. That firm always employed good Canadian citizens of Hamilton,

Supply-Im migration
and I believe they have been driven out of business because of the fact that we have permitted to come into the country sweat shop labour that we cannot assimilate into our population, and with which our own people cannot compete.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the long explanation given by the minister and I must confess that I have yet no clear conception of what he has done or what he proposes to do with reference to this problem. I believe that we are entering an era in the history of this country when we require for our proper development something new in the shape of an aggressive immigration policy; we need measures that are vigorous and bold. We have to take a chance if we are to succeed; we cannot sit down and rely on old methods and the course of nature if we are to secure the population which we so much require. I know of a scheme which has been before the department for at least a year and which involved the bringing into Canada of the most desirable type of settlers from the north of Scotland, from the Hebrides, but I have reason to believe that these settlers have not yet been secured, although at least a thousand of them could have been brought in in the last year. Why has not this been done? I cannot understand why we should suffer from a moment's delay in this regard. We want people in this country of the right sort and we should not hesitate a moment in seizing an opportunity to bring in a dozen, a hundred, or a thousand men who will make desirable citizens.
With the majority of the members of this House, I regard farming as our basic industry; and so far as I can gather from the minister's policy he purposes to look for agricultural immigrants from foreign countries. True, he states that the British will be given the preference. But what steps is he going to take to bring people from the British Isles into Canada? I have waited for some explanation as to why such a small amount is spent in advertising in Great Britain in comparison with such a tremendous sum in foreign countries. That explanation has been promised but so far it is not forthcoming, and I think that this House might have expected it almost forthwith, after the suggestion that was made that enough was not being spent in Great Britain. In my opinion it is possible to secure desirable settlers from Great Britain for farming purpose-I have given one instance of where there are farmers available for- this country who have not been brought in.

I am glad to know that some steps are being taken in this direction, but at the same time I want to impress upon the minister the fact that our people are anxious to increase the 54 per cent of Anglo-Saxons who now reside in Canada. And we can do this by a proper, aggressive campaign for immigrants from Great Britain. I do not know whether a suggestion from me is of any use, but I cannot see why we should not inform the British government and our agents in Great Britain that we are prepared to take in this country 100,000, or as many as they like to send, of the youth of Great Britain from the ages of fourteen to sixteen or seventeen. The Canadian government could take the responsibility of placing them on proper farms and carrying out a system of inspection oi these farms to see that these youths were properly educated, and there might be, in connection with a scheme of this kind, a regular annual examination, so that these boys, when they qualified under tests prescribed by the Department of Agriculture, or whatever department was selected, might be enabled to secure land of their own and '

be encouraged to develop it. By so doing I believe we could form the foundation in this country of such a future as we cannot expect if we bring in undesirable immigrants from foreign countries.
The same poilcy should be adopted for our cities. I think, with the hon. member (Mr. Hoey), that there should be co-operation between our Department of Immigration and the various municipal councils. But I would go further. We have in every city and town social service organizations such as Rotary and Kiwanis clubs, Y.M.C.A.'s and church associations, every one of which is directly interested in the development of this country. I would advocate that we carry on a campaign of education among these organizations 'with a view to impressing upon them the great importance to Canada's welfare of increasing our population by the addition of the right sort of people. And I believe that if proper steps were taken to co-operate with these organizations we could secure the results we desire.
We have placed before us briefly three views: one, no restrictions; two, no immigrants; three, selected immigrants. I want to support my argument for selected immigrants, and for immigrants as largely as possible from the British Isles, with some figures giving the experience of the United States. They have gone through a period in their history similar to what we will go through in the next hundred years. They have had the experience, let us benefit by that experience. What I am about to quote is the result of their experience gained from scientific tests made by them during the war. Scientific mental tests were made on 1,700,000 officers and men of the American expeditionary force. This is a quotation from the official army mental tests:
Relatively early in this supreme struggle, it became clear to certain individuals that the proper utilization of man-power, and more particularly of mind or brainpower, would assure ultimate victory. . . All this had to be done in the least possible time. Never before in the history of civilization was brain, as contrasted with brawn, so important; never before, the proper placement and utilization of brain-power so essential to success.
Our War Department, nerved to exceptional risks by the stem necessity for early victory, saw and immediately seized its opportunity to develop various new lines of personnel work. Among these is numbered the psychological service. Great will be our good fortune if the lesson in human engineering which the war has taught is carried over directly and effectively into our civil institutions and activities.
The purposes of these psychologcal tests were, as stated in the army orders: "(a) to aid in segregating the mentally incompetent, (b) to classify men according to their mental capacity, (c) to assist in selecting competent men for responsible positions." And, to quote

I should like to refer to a remark made, I think, either by the minister himself (Mr. Stewart) or by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke), that the Londoner cannot stand the conditions on our farms.

Then it was the leader of the Progressive party. I take issue with him. While the Londoner of mature age may not make a good farmer, still the youth born in London will if he is properly trained. I be-

lieve the Londoner can be trained to do anything. Many of us saw the Londoner on the field of battle, and we also saw him living under conditions that no farmer in this country has ever had to endure-sleeping in the mud and on ice with nothing under him but a waterproof sheet. And he stood it. We must not belittle the Anglo-Saxon, the British, because I feel that the United States have proved beyond all question that the immigrant of Anglo-Saxon stock makes the best citizen. He is the dominant influence in the United States to-day. In my opinion the only way in which we can make this country prosperous and have a national type with a proper patriotism is to follow the policy of bringing the Britisher to this country and thus making Canada a British nation instead of the conglomerate nation we shall be if we persist in the policy of bringing in foreigners.

Mr. Chairman, I am not entering this debate with any thought of delaying the estimates, nor of embarrassing the minister, but to offer what little I can to solve what seems to be a very difficult problem. I am glad to speak for a moment, if it is only to congratulate the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) on the excellent address he gave the committee a few moments ago. I was very glad to hear what he said, because after I had visualized the picture drawn by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) last night I feared that one of the factors in the prosperity of the city from which I come was about to disappear entirely.

Mr. Chairman, if I may be allowed a question. Is not the hon. gentleman aware-I am quite sure the hon. member for Springfield is-that the crop of which we have a record in the Manitoba Free Press for 1921 fell below the taxes of the province by over $16,000,000?
Mr. Chairman, I was not referring to an isolated statement of that kind at all.
But that is the fact.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I was referring to the statement my hon. friend made last night that his province was practically bankrupt. And people who are bankrupt cannot buy goods.
We are not buying them, either.

I think it is hardly necessary to argue that immigration is desirable, although I know there are elements in this

House that are rather unfriendly to the idea of bringing more people into this country. I do not think the point needs labouring that we want more people. In a country of the size of Canada, with its illimitable resources, the question of the need of more people should not be open to argument at all. But if in working out the details, the minister finds that he is meeting with a good deal of difficulty and some opposition, I would say to him, if I may, that in this parliament as elsewhere, it is absolutely impossible always to reconcile the ideas of various people, and he should go on just as he thinks is in the interest of the people of Canada. When I say that, I would also say-and I will refer to this later-that I do not entirely agree with one or two of the suggestions which he has in mind.
The value of immigration cannot be minimised. It develops our natural resources, in the first place. The greater 'the number of people you have in the country, the greater the consumption and therefore, the greater will be the production required. Thus, the question whether we should have more people in this country with its great spaces and its resources should not be open to argument. There are certain facts operating against the success of immigration at the present time, even if we open the door very wide. The first thing is the high cost of transportation. The people of the British Isles, and the people of European continental countries as-well, are not blessed with a great deal of this world's goods. In many instances, they have not the money, even if they so desire, to pay their way across the ocean. In past years those immigrants who have come to Canada-and I Have knowledge of some of them-have come here because their friends or relatives in this country have advanced them the money to pay for transportation. The second reason is this, that in the past two years the restrictions have been so onerous that it has been impossible for those people to come. While some of those restrictions have, I am glad to say, been removed by the present government-and I am in this making no special criticism of the previous government- the effects of those restrictions are still occupying the minds of people who would like to come. There are, I understand, people today in England and on the European continent who believe it is impossible for them to enter Canada, who believe that the restrictions which existed at one time are still in force. A vigorous immigration policy would include making known to the people whom we wish to secure the fact that they -would be welcome if they desired to come to Canada. For that

I would spend a little money; I would not spend a great deal. I may say frankly and almost at the outset that I am in favour of voluntary immigration. I am not particularly enamoured-and I say this with all goodwill *-of any scheme which contemplates the expenditure of great sums of money to induce . people to come to Canada, and perhaps, painting rosier pictures than should be painted. I am also not very greatly in favour of spending large amounts of money on those people after they arrive in Canada. Briefly, I would say this. I would spend a reasonable sum of money in acquainting the people of various countries from which we wish to attract immigrants, with the fact that if they are willing to work, if they are healthy, if they are white, if they are morally and physically sound, we shall be glad, to welcome them to this country and to open the door to them.
I might say, just in passing, in reply to the speech of the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Clark) that I am quite in sympathy with him w'hen he says that we ought to encourage immigration from the British Isles. I believe, however, if we desire to obtain all the immigration which this country ought to have and which it can stand, we cannot stop there.
What class of men -would the hon. member bring from the British Isles?

I was coming to that a little later on; but. I would say to my hon. friend that I would not bar a man whether he was a farmer or engaged in any other occupation, provided that he was physically, mentally and morally fit. I was going to refer for a moment to some of the remarks made by one or two hon. members opposite, and more particularly to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). Last evening, when I was listening to him, I felt rather depressed and discouraged for fear that what he said might possibly be true, although I could hardly believe it. I was, for that reason, particularly pleased that the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) took up the cudgels on behalf of the western provinces and said what he did.
I would not like the hon. member to go on record in that way. Every word of what I said was true, and the hon. member for Springfield admitted that quite possibly it was true in Alberta.

I did not hear the hon. member for Springfield admit that the West was bankrupt. In discussing western Canada and the life of the farmer there, I say with all sincerity-and I think my hon. friends will 78i
believe me-that those who come from industrial Ontario have every sympathy with the western farmer, and I believe we are willing to go almost any distance in a reasonable way to help them, if giving such assistance is possible. In saying that, I am thinking now of another farming district in Ontario. I come from the county of Waterloo, the centre of a farming and industrial district in western Ontario. I believe that there we have, perhaps, the happiest combination, the combination that makes for success. We have an industrial population, manufacturing towns and cities surounded by good farming country in which mixed farming is being carried on. If that could be developed in western Canada, I think the problem that is being discussed would be solved.
Would the hon. member tell us where the farmers would find a market for products from mixed farming?

I was coming to that. That deals very intimately with the question of immigration of which we are speaking now. That is why I am in favour of immigration for the West as well as for other parts of Canada. I was going to make a comparison. In western Ontario, the part of the province from which I come we have first-class agricultural land. In Western Canada, I fear it is true that many of the farmers, particularly in southern Alberta, from what I have heard, have become located on land which will never be able to support them as an agricultural community. That will correct itself in time. Apparently, the. greatest difficulty they have is their distance from the *market. The population is not there to consume that which they themselves p duce, and they are forced to the necessity of exporting their goods by rail for some thousand or fifteen hundred miles and then overseas to foreign markets. I am not a pessimist when I say this, but this has often occurred to me when the difficulties of the western farmer have been discussed: I am not sure whether the West, in the matter of growing wheat and exporting it thousands of miles to the country of consumption, is not at the present moment conducting what is really a great experiment. I do not know whether it is possible for western Canada to continue to grow wheat only and to send it to market, this requiring the expenditure of large sums of money for transportation, something which cannot be overcome at the present time. It must be difficult to carry this on, because the western farmers are in competition with countries where wheat can

be produced at low prices and transported at lower costs.
Is the hon. member aware that the best British economists inform us that wheat consumption in Europe to-day is only one-third of what it would normally be if Europe were re-established?

That is, in a way, an answer to my question. When the European peoples become able again to purchase to the full extent of their requirements, the price of wheat will go up, and that will immediately be reflected in the prosperity of the western farmer. Let us hope that that condition will soon come about.
" A good time coming

In the meantime the eastern farmer has his local market, and I am inclined to believe-I do not care to be dogmatic with regard to these things-that that which makes the eastern farmer prosperous will be what in the end will have to make the western farmer prosperous, and that is the development of a home market.
Does the hon. member consider that the eastern farmer is prosperous to-day?
I am speaking now for the farmers in my own community. Perhaps when I use the word " prosperous", I use too strong a word.
Hear, hear.

I am not going to' say I used too strong a word. I said " perhaps ". I do say this, that the farmers in the neighbourhood in which I live are very comfortable. They produce a great many of the things which they need; they produce a variety of commodities-butter, cheese, eggs, wheat, and the other products that are raised in western Ontario, and which they take to the towns and industrial centres. The point I want to make is that the interests of the cities and towns are identical with theirs, the farmer gets his home market there, and the working man living in the towns and cities gets the benefit of having these goods brought in to him from time to time. I believe that that will be the salvation of the West. Perhaps I should not say the salvation, but I believe that is the proper solution of their problem. When the hon. member for Springfield spoke of the development of a water power in Manitoba great-enough to move the wheels of vast industries, I was hoping that at no distant time the West itself would begin to create its own industrial centres, and then the problem of the farmers

will be solved if they apply themselves diligently to farming as farming ought to be carried out, and do not try to spread themselves over too much territory, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Springfield.
What is "too much"?

If it is true that the western . lands, as in some cases has been mentioned, are not in a position to produce crops, if that should turn out to be the general condition in the West, which I do not believe, then I do not see how any legislation on the part of this or any other government can relieve the situation. I am not referring particularly to the tariff. I know my western friends would like to have the tariff reduced, and in some cases entirely wiped out. I come from an industrial community. Some 150 to 175 manufacturing establishments are operating in the town from which I come, and I say to my hon. friends, if it is of any interest to them to have me say it, I am not a high protectionist. I have the good of the industries at heart.
I do not wish to see them destroyed.
Can my hon. friend mention any member of this House who is a high protectionist?
I think that almost anybody in the chamber is as capable of forming an opinion with regard to that as I am.
Then the hon. member is not in sympathy with the tariff plank in the Liberal platform of 1919.

I do not know just exactly what the hon. member is driving at, but I will say quite frankly that I at no time approved of the tariff plank in the Liberal platform.
I was making a comparison between the eastern farmer, and the western farmer, and for that reason I did not think it necessary to discuss the tariff in this connection for the simple reason that the tariff applies to the eastern farmer just as it does to the western farmer. If the trouble, then, is with the markets, they must find their market in the United States where there are great centres of population nearer to them, or else build a market of their own. The latter takes time and immigration, and that is my sole reason for referring to the West and western conditions in this way.

How would it be possible for the West to build up industrial centres without some form of protection against the highly developed industrialism of Ontario and Quebec?

There is no reason in the world why the west could not develop industries just as Ontario has done. I can see no point in that argument.

The hon. gentleman seems
to be anxious to protect the industries of his own town against the industries of the United States. Have we of the West not the same right to be anxious concerning the highly developed industries of Ontario?

I cannot grasp the hon. member's solicitude for the industries of western Ontario. I do not see why in the course of time western Canada, which is under exactly the same economic conditions as eastern Canada so far as the tariff is concerned, cannot develop industries in the same way as western Ontario has developed them, or Quebec, or any other part of Canada. Perhaps I am very slow in grasping the point of the hon. gentleman.

I wish I could put the question a little more clearly, because it is vital. How does the hon. member expect western Canada to develop industries without some form of protection against the highly developed industries of Ontario?
In exactly the same way as, to-day, a small manufacturer can begin his industry in Ontario and build it up in competition with the larger ones.

Why, then, do the Ontario
manufacturers need protection against the United States manufacturers?

I did not propose to get into a debate on the tariff, though I am not at all afraid of debating the tariff. As I said, I am not a high protectionist, or perhaps I might say, as one hon. gentleman said once, I am not a very high protectionist. The one answer to that question, and I propose then to go on with my argument, is this: As against the United States you have a population of 120,000,000 to compete with. Their manufacturers have a market of 120,000,000 of people as compared with the 8,000,000 of people that the Canadian manufacturer has for his market. I will say this, and leave it at that:	I believe there are many manufacturers in Canada to-day-and I know some of them in my own community-who would be willing to enter into open competition on an equal basis with the United States manufacturer if the tariff wall came down both ways. But to ask the Canadian manufacturer to throw his market open to the highly developed industries of the United States, with their big home market, and not have
access to that market himself, that, I say is not a fair and square deal.
They are ready for reciprocity.

Now, I think I might be permitted to go on with my real argument.
I have said that I favoured a form of voluntary immigration with no great amount of money expended in bringing the people here, but I would like to make known to them that they could come, and that we would welcome them -when they did come. I would open the door reasonably wide with proper precautions. I would let in the man who looks like a worker, though I agree with the hon. member for Springfield that it might be pretty difficult to say whether a man is an earnest worker or not, but where there was any doubt I would be inclined to give the immigrant the benefit of the doubt.
I think there are certain things that are fundamental in the discussion of this question. First of all, the immigrant should be physically healthy, mentally and morally healthy. Secondly, there should be a certain racial fitness, and in that I am not going so far perhaps as some others; when I speak of that, I would say that I would exclude the oriental; I would go that far, and not a great deal further. And then there should be a certain industrial fitness, although I think that is of minor importance.
Now, some of the non-essentials as I view them are these: I would not insist on any great money qualification. If this country had insisted on immigrants having a certain amount of money in their pockets upon arrival, I wonder how many of us would be here to-day. I think the forefathers, the fathers and grandfathers, of a great many of us, would not have been able to come to Canada if there had been any money test at that time. I am glad that requirement has now been removed. I do not think the matter of language is so important; that will correct itself in one generation. I further think that the matter of occupation is not of very great importance either, because if we enforce too many restrictions, if we ask too many questions of these people as to what they are going to do, exactly what man they are going to be employed with, and all the rest of it, the impression will remain in the European countries and in Britain that it is difficult to enter Canada, and a great many people whom it would be desirable to have come here would not even attempt to enter. So I say that if men fill all the requirements of which I have spoken I would let them enter Canada no
