During the past few weeks when reading the newspapers I was in hopes that peace was in sight in Ireland. But after hearing the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoev), I have decided that the prospect is' hopeless. In regard to this important subject that is now being discussed I was just a little disappointed in the spech of that hon. member. I will tell you why. My hon. friend mentioned immigration, and also spoke af the economic factors that entered into the life of the WTest, but devoted practically the whole of his time to the subject of immigration. I wish he had devoted his fine talents to solving the economic difficulties that are the real' cause of our dissatisfaction at the present time.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) made the statement that the West needs salvation. By implication he admits that the conditions are not what they should be in the West, and in speaking of the conditions of Canada in general and the subject of immigration he naturally spoke of the brotherhood of man. I wonder whether the brotherhood of man takes in the black man and the yellow race as well as the white race. Of course, I do not believe in these people being admitted here, but it seems to me to be a little inconsistent, when you are speaking of the brotherhood of man and the equality of man, to discriminate against those races. I+ may be that some time in the near future it will be difficult for us to discriminate against those nations which are becoming enlightened forces in the world at the present time. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) spoke of British immigration. So far as that question is concerned, he has my sympathy. I believe to a large extent that a British country, or a country that was settled by the
British to a large extent, should be populated by that stock, and for that reason I am in sympathy with what the hon. member said in regard to that policy.
I was very much impressed with the very excellent and most extraordinary speech of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). In the first place it was excellent in preparation, excellent in delivery and most extraordinary in the revelation that he gave to this House last night. He qualified his statement to some extent by saying that he was dealing largely with the conditions in his own constituency, and I have it on the authority of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) that a part of my own constituency is really in a -worse condition than the constituency of the hon. member for Bow River. But after I got home last night, feeling depressed with the situation, I came to the conclusion that it was not the part of wisdom to generalize and to say that the whole of western Canada was in the same condition, because we do know that in certain portions of the West it is possible at least to make a comfortable living. As far as my own constituency is concerned, I do not say that the fault lies with this administration, but it seems to me a great fault lies at the feet of the governments who opened up large areas of land that should never have been opened. That is one of the problems of the West. Lands that should have always remained ranch lands should never have been opened for homesteading. If I shut my eyes for a moment I can see a stretch of a hundred miles in my own constituency that
5 p.m. to-day is largely becoming a barren wilderness, and yet fifteen years ago it was the most productive part of my constituency. The government opened mile after mile of land until they got a little too near the hills, with the result that after the prairie grass and shrubbery were taken off the hills, the wind played havoc with the soil, and smothered the valley with sand, till to-day, if you drive through with a motor car, you will find the fences covered with it. So that the fault was not altogether with the country, but the trouble arose because of the opening of certain territories which should never have been opened to the settler.
I am glad to see there is a remedy in view, and the government to a large extent have advocated that remedy. There is a scheme on foot by which those good settlers who are acclimatized and experienced shall be taken off those bad lands and transferred to lands more favourable to the diversified agriculture
Supply-Immigration

which we advocate in Saskatchewan. With reference to the remedy which the hop. member for Bow River emphasized last night, I am entirely in accord, but I am not in accord with the general conditions. However, I agree with the remedy which he advocated and emphasized. There is one point upon which I differ, and I differ because of what I heard this afternoon. He made a quotation from a statement of the Bishop of Birmingham, to the effect that the British race were being sent to the colonies to re-ftivigorate them. Well, if the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) and the hon. member for Bow River, are samples of the stock they are sending here to be re-invigorated, I do not think that the British nation is going to become defunct, or that they are in a state of decay or in need of regeneration.
How about yourself?

That is all right, The hon.
member for Springfield said that in a careful analysis of western conditions we should discriminate between the economic factors that are entering into the situation and the country at large. I quite agree with him. I am quite in accord, and I do not play second fiddle to any one in regard to eulogies of the West. I think it is a splendid country. I think it has the most productive soil of any country in the world.
Hear, hear.

Nobody denies that. We are not denying that. We can produce 400,000,000 bushels of wheat in the coming year, as far as that is concerned. But in spite of the fact that we have the finest land and can produce the best wheat in the world, to a large extent we are not prosperous and many people are leaving us. Therefore, what we say is not that the land is not good or that there is anything wrong with the country, but that there must be something wrong with our internal policy which makes conditions as they are.

Are the people all right
out there?

The people that we have, yes. But- some of the people who come to us are not always the best.
The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) spoke of the literature that was sent to the Old Country. I remember, twenty years ago, receiving this very literature. I admit it was a little exaggerated, but I am not sorry that I came to this country. I am glad that I came. The hon. member 
for Springfield tells us about coming to this country and working his way through university. I may tell him that I was in the same position when I came to Canada. I took the first job offered to me. I was told I had an appointment in Winnipeg when I came here, but I found the agent was lying to me. I simply settled down and took the first job I could get. After a number of years I saved enough to take a university and theological course, and I had a wife and family at the same time. Any country where there is this possibility of a man of ambition getting through, I think, is a worth-while country. There is nothing wrong with the country. But it is probably our internal conditions that make it what it is at the present time. In the matter of comparison can you compare Canada with Germany, where we are told economic conditions are terrible and people are hardly able to live, or with Russia where conditions are so bad-with apologies for the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). In those countries, there seems to be economic chaos. As far as other countries are concerned, with the one exception of the United States, it seems to me at the present time that Canada is the finest country in the world.

Why except the United
States?

At the present time it seems to me that the conditions in the United States, with its internal policy, are possibly a little better for the people who want to create desirable home conditions. The climate is not so severe and industrial conditions in that country seem to give better scope for men who are seeking employment. Of course, from the point of view of my wife and family, I would say that Canada is the best.
Let me say a few words in regard to the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Rinfret). I always listen to that hon. gentleman with marked attention. He generally has a prepared address and we usually expect something worth while from him. But his immigration policy I do not agree with. He said he was willing to let any people come into Canada from any country in the world. That statement, I think, is far too general. The hon. member sympathises with the minister and the government because he says there are so many contradictory views placed before parliament on this subject that it is very difficult to know where one stands. It seems to me, however, that he rather increased the contradiction. There is one thing he did say that struck me and that was that the reason

Supply-Immigration
for immigration was obvious. I listened to learn just wherein it was so obvious, and the hon. gentleman explained himself. In the first place, he said, immigration was to help the people who are now in the country to bear the burden of the national debt; secondly, it was to assist our National Railways; and in the third place it was intended to increase our wealth. Now, I do not think that any one of these three things is the real reason why we should get people to come into Canada. You tell the people of other lands that you want them to help bear the national debt, to assist the railways out of their difficulties, and to contribute towards our wealth, and they will look for some other field for their activities. It is easy to see, of course, that if you increase the number of people in the country and divide the debt amongst ' them you will decrease it proportionately. But I do not see how, if the wealth in Canada today is stationary, you are going to increase it by bringing more people into the country, when at the same time that increase in population means a decrease in the debt. It does not appear to me to be logical that in one direction you decrease the national debt by bringing in more people and, in another, you increase the wealth by the same means. The hon. member also referred to emigration to the United States. He did not say whether the figures were correct, but no doubt they were approximately so. He gave a cure for this outward flow of people; he said that it lay in an increase in the number of immigrants coming into the country. And he was surprised at the' opposition of the farmers to farm labourers coming into Canada. Now, so far as my hon. friend for Springfield is concerned, in view of the conditions in Manitoba, there may be room for immigrants there; and if the people in that province are in such circumstances that they can assimilate farm labourers and take care of them in winter they should do so. But, speaking for my own constituency, I must say that during the winter we have not even enough work for our own boys who are living on our farms to-day, and I do certainly hope that there will be found some solution whereby the western farmer can be enabled to make ends meet.
Now a word or two with regard to the statement that we need a class of immigrants from northern Europe to go into northern Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the observation that came from across the floor that this class of people will exist where the average Canadian would perish. I do not think that it would be the best" plan to bring such people into the country. It
may be that we can get a class of settlers who will establish themselves on such lands as are evidently in contemplation. But I see a difficulty; how are you going to keep them there? Let me state my own experience. We have certain people of that description whom we settled in Saskatchewan; and what do we do immediately we find them there? The different churches-and I am speaking of my own church as well-immediately look over the situation from the home mission standpoint, see that these people are isolated, and go to them with this statement, "Why, you have not the facilities for education that you should have." Then what action do we take? We make our appeal and gather money from East and West and in Saskatoon, Prince Albert and other places we build what are called "school homes." We then educate the most favoured and the soundest of these boys at the home in Saskatoon and in immediate proximity to the collegiate and the university, and after we have educated them we find that instead of going back to their own people as we had expected, they enter into our professions and defeat the very object for which we had them educated. So that in the ultimate analysis the people do not settle at all. The older generation stay there, but the younger generation, of whom we say that our democracy should be built up, will not stay under these conditions. So that unless we loop the loop every ten years by resettling that northern country, this kind of education and settlement is not advantageous to the Canadian people at large.
I do not wish to speak at any great length on this subject, but there is one thing that was said by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) with reference to children who might be brought into this country. He presented one phase of the argument against the bringing in of these children by almost casting a blot on our national life. He spoke about the number of babies that died under one year of age in Quebec, Ontario, and all through the list of the provinces. Now, I have had some experience so far as this is concerned, and I am convinced that the death rate in Canada of children under one year compares favourably with that of any other country in the world. We all admit that some children die under that age, but we could not rear them all; that has never yet been done. So that there is no argument in that respect against bringing children into the country. There is, however, an argument against such immigration, in that, as it seems to me, during the period of adolescence these children should have at least the influence of a real home under the care of father and mother
Supply-Immigration

and not be subject entirely to the influence of strangers.
Now I come to what I think is the crux of the whole problem. Why is such a desperate effort being made to-day to secure immigration to Canada? That seems to me to be the crux of the entire situation. I am not against immigration to Canada. Not at all. I believe that ambitious young men and women should come to this country, and I think that there is plenty of room for them. But why this desperate effort? If conditions in the country were all right and people here were satisfied I have no doubt that they would tell their friends just how things were. But it does seem to me that there is something wrong with our internal policy when we find it necessary to make such strenuous efforts to secure people. We are told that the United States to-day has received almost its full quota of immigration from the British Isles, although it has no special immigration policy. The United States does not make any particular plea for people to come in. The only reason I can see why people go to the United States is that immigrants who go there are so satisfied with the internal conditions and the economic life of the country, and find that there is such a possibility of making a home, that through their own propaganda other people are attracted to the country.
My hon. friend the member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler), who is in his seat at the moment, made a very fine speech, but there was one thing he bemoaned. He said that if we do not get immigration to this country we shall soon be out of existence. I am surprised at the hon. member making that statement. If it came from British Columbia, where it seems face suicide is on the increase, it would be all right; but it seems out of place coming from the province of Quebec, which I think is doing her duty towards the national life of Canada. I might say myself that I do not believe there is any danger of our going out of existence. Fifteen years ago there were only myself and my wife; now we are ten.
Hear, hear.

So I do not think there is any danger of our passing out of existence for some time. But after carefully looking over the arguments of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I am led to this conclusioli, that he contends that the prosperity of Canada, industrial, economic and social, depends entirely on the prosperity of agriculture. I think that is a right conclusion to draw from his speech. If it is wrong I hope he will say so.

I do not think my hon.
friend is quite right. I said that agriculture was tributary to the cities, and that you had to have a properly balanced population. I think the rural population should be greater than the urban in a country of this description. They should be balanced; that is my argument.
I accept my hon. friend's statement, but it does seem to me he went further and said that the basis of the prosperity of our industrial life depended upon the prosperity of agriculture.

I admit that. I think it
does in this country.
Then I think we are agreed that the success of agriculture is essential to the well-being of the whole of Canada.
Hear, hear.

Now, I want to ask: Is immigration going to assist agriculture? Are we making one step in the right direction co that the prosperity of agriculture may become the basis of the well-being of Canada? That is the only question I wish to ask. I shall try to answer it in a few moments.
There is one other subject I wish to speak upon in passing, and that is the deporting of immigrants. Recently I was speaking to a clergyman who seine time ago went over to the Old Land. He told me that he decided to take a berth in the steerage because he found there were on board thirty-three or thirty-four British immigrants who were being deported. He spoke to these people and found among them a Scotchman, a very strong man physically and apparently mentally sound. He had had a position offered to him in Canada, but for some reason on arrival he was detained, later placed behind bars, and in a month's time deported. That man was a veteran of the Great Wrar and had received honour at the hands of the British authorities. When he tells his own people in Scotland of his deportation it is safe to assume that any intending immigrants to this country after hearing his story will change their plans and go to the United States.

One hon. member speaking about the causes of failure said there were

two: one, over-purchase of land; the other, heavy overhead expenses. Are these the real causes of the difficulty in which our agriculturists find themselves at the present time? I do not think this is the trouble in Saskatchewan; it may be in Manitoba where holdings of two sections are said to be common, but the great majority of the people where I live in Saskatchewen-and I am acquainted with over 1,000 families-farm a half-section which I do not think is too large. Consequently I do not believe that the two causes mentioned are responsible for the general failure of agriculturists in the West.
I think the hon. minister (Mr. Stewart) in speaking of colonization said he hoped his scheme would enable men to be settled within eighteen to thirty miles of railway facilities where they could engage in mixed farming.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not thirty miles; up to fifteen.

I thank the minister for the correction. I believe that mixed farming is going to be one of the main solutions of the difficulties of Saskatchewan farmers at all events. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) in speaking of the solution of the problems confronting this country said that free trade would ruin the East and he voiced the opinion that the kind of people wanted here was domestic servants and labourers with pick and shovel. I believe that m this discrimination between men engaged in manual work and professional men there is a false philosophy which sooner or later will drive our highly organized society to the wall. I remember some years ago in the University of Saskatchewan coming in contact with men who thought that because a man had a university education he had a right to a better home than the man who worked in the sewers, for instance. It seems to me that the man who works in the sewers, who, as we say, does the dirty work, is far more in need of recreation and the luxuries of home than the professional man; and I think the sooner we as a democracy realize that the health and sanity of this nation depend to a large extent upon the groundwork, the so-called dirty work of looking after our sewers and so forth, the better it will be for all concerned. The sooner we educate the people that any honest work is worthy of a place of honour in our society, the sooner we shall recognize that there must be a commensurate reward for the proper discharge of the disagreeable work of the community.
Quite right.

In my constituency of Swift Current we had a class of people who are called Mennonites. I understand from the Minister of Agriculture and from the people around Swift Current that the}' were the best class of farmers to be found in the district. They were making good, and yet for some reason or other they in a body went to Mexico. We do not believe that the Mexican conditions are better than our own, and yet as far as I am able to discover we did not turn a hand to try and stop this exodus. They may not be ideal citizens in conforming to our educational laws, but they are amongst the very best farmers to be found anywhere.
Now, I do not think it would be wise on my part to take up the time of this House without offering some solution of the problem that confronts us. In this connection I do not want to be hard on the government,. The Acting Minister of Immigration has my sympathy, but I have listened for a definite policy of immigration, and so far as I can gather it seems to be this. When we, as representing the farmers speak in regard to the tariff, rve are told that the government listens first- of all to the manufacturers to see if it is possible for them to do without certain protection that we wish to have removed. That may be the right course to pursue. The manufacturers understand manufacturing conditions better than we do, and therefore the government may be justified in listening to them. In the same way it seems to me that when we, who are agriculturists, come down to this liouse and describe the conditions of agriculture, an industry in whose success we are personally interested, the government should listen to our representations. But instead of taking the advice of those who are on the spot and experienced in agricultural conditions, the government listens to someone else. The same may be said in regard to labour. Labour has its representatives here who tell us that they do not need any industrial immigrants. Do we take any notice of what they say? I did not think that all the wisdom of the sages was monopolized by the capitalistic and manufacturing classes-not by any means. I think it will be found that the greatest men that have ever lived have all sprung from the farm. For that reason, it seems to me, it behooves the government to listen to the agriculturists as regards their conditions and the solution of their problems.	-
I will close by speaking briefly regarding three things. If I were to be asked what I consider would be one way to improve the condition of the West, I believe the remedy and immigration should come in at the same
Supply-Immigration

time. I do not include one to the exclusion of the other. We should have people coming in because, in my constituency, you have a school, you have taxation, and if people leave the land, the burden on the few that remain becomes intolerable. Therefore, if people are moving from this country, we must have other people to take their place. But at the same time, we should have a remedy that will cause people to remain in this country. One of the solutions of the problem is, I think, this. I am not speaking of agricultural implements, and I am speaking directly now to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I would place the absolute necessaries of life on the free trade list, and I would also remove the sales tax and give the people who are endeavouring to make a home an opportunity to establish themselves on the land. That would be one of the remedies that I would advocate and I give that advice to the government.
The second, it seems to me, the hon. member for Springfield just touched on, and that is the lack of co-operation amongst the whole people of Canada. What I mean by that is this. I think it was found some time ago by investigation that, as regards a hundred commodities that enter into the national wellbeing of the people of this country, the factory price was forty cents on the dollar, but sixty cents was taken up before an article got into the hands of the consumer. That is "over-commercialization," if you can use that term. I have seen it in my village, a village with two stores, and the commercial men crowding on each other at the rate of five or six a day, selling brooms, bluing, washing machines and so on. It seems to me that we are overrun with that class of people who are taking out a picking, in the middleman sense, before an article gets to the consumer. I am not saying that the manufacturer charges too much for his commodity; perhaps he does not; but before an article gets to the consumer, instead of costing forty cents, it costs one dollar. What we are kicking against at the present time is this lack of co-operation, and if some means could be devised by which we could eliminate many of these middlemen, commercial men and selling' agents, and lower freight rates I believe one of the greatest problems that enter into the production of our western lands would be solved.
I do not know that I should presume to give advice to the government; but this is my final statement. If I were asked to go into a business, first of all I would look into that business to see if it was solvent, if there was any danger of bankruptcy. If I found that
[Mr. Lewis.!
the business was exceeding its revenue, I would think twice before going in. We have the great business of Canada, nationalizing our assets, our industrial life and our agricultural life, and we are inviting people to come to this country. They look into the situation and the financial state of Canada, and they find that we as a government-and I include myself in this parliament-are exceeding our revenue in the administration of our work by over $40,000,000 or $50,000,000, as the case may be. If we as a people want to get people to come from different parts of the world, people who are intelligent, who can discriminate, then let us clean house in this parliament; let us, as a nation, begin to live within our income, and the time will not be long before we hear once again the tramp of feet of people coming to our shores, and the laughter of the children in the many homes that are found within the borders of Canada.

A consideration of the matter involved in this appropriation is one of the most important that could engage the attention of this parliament. The problems involved, which have been discussed by various hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate, are of the most vital character; they strike at the existing condition of affairs in this country. It is, therefore, quite right that we should have had such a full discussion as we have had, and I hope the discussion will go on until all hon. members may deal with this question from their various points of view. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) and the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) who preceded him from the other side of the House are, I think, to be congratulated on the fact that they have lifted the debate to a much higher level than that on which it stood yesterday., I did not have an opportunity of hearing the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland); but on reading over his remarks, I began to wonder whether he really belonged to a party which called itself "Progressive", because if there ever was a misnomer as regards the application of the term "progressive" to that hon. gentleman as a member of that party, then I am sure it revealed itself last night. Rather, he might be said to belong to a "retrograde" or " pessimistic" party, in whose make-up no vestige of progressiveness could be found. When the hon. member for Springfield and the hon. member for Swift Current manfully and courageously faced and laid before us the real situation in the country and discussed the matter in a practical way, I am sure the House and the country felt gratified at their contribution to this debate.

Supply-Immigration
Everybody must recognize that the situation in Canada to-day is one which demands the closest possible attention and the wisest judgment on the part of every hon. gentleman who happens to represent in this House any portion of the people of Canada. We are confronted by great problems which one might enumerate at length; but I need only mention the fact that the problem of taxation which bears upon the wage earner, the farmer, the artisan, in fact, every man in every occupation in life, is of so severe a character that how we are going to deal with that problem and how we can reach the stage and time in our history when we may be relieved in some degree of that burden, is a matter which is of great importance, not only to ourselves, but to those who come after us in this country. That problem is not to be faced by sitting down and declaring that this is the worst country in the world because hon. gentlemen who use that argument in discussing this question, utterly fail to pay the slightest attention to conditions which exist elsewhere. My hon. friend (Mr. Garland) who came from across the ocean, knows that the land from which he came is to-day suffering under difficulties and conditions a thousand times worse than those that exist in Canada. If you take the whole of Europe, the situation there was well described a few days ago by Hilaire Belloc, speaking in Montreal, when he discussed the possible fate of civilization which at the moment was hanging in the balance in Europe, and pointed out conditions that existed. If that is so in other parts of the world, why should hon. gentlemen in this House undertake to tell a pitiful story of exaggeration as to conditions that happen to be found in one locality due to drought, and the continued failure of crops on account of like conditions, and lead the House and the country to believe that Canada is in a desperate condition, because that happens to be the situation in one particular part of this country?
We have our difficulties in the East. Our farmers and wage earners have problems of a more or less grave character; but where do these problems come from? They come from the reaction which followed the war in a very great degree. Nowadays, we are all too apt to think that the solution of matters that come up for consideration to-day can be determined by the wisdom which we possess for the moment, and that we must not look at the story of the past or the lessons of history in order to find out whether or not in the days that have gone, the people that have gone before, have had similar problems
to deal with. What was the situation in Great Britain after the great Napoleonic wars? Let me call the attention of the committee to a very short statement regarding that published in an admirable work, written by Mr. Marriott, M.A., Professor of History in the University of Oxford, and. entitled England Since Waterloo.
The human heart through all the ages that have gone has always remained the same. Problems of a different nature would recur throughout the ages and they were solved by the wise men of those days but in the century following probably exactly the same problem would arise under different conditions varying according to the country where it did arise, and would have to be dealt with along the same lines. One might think to hear hon. gentlemen talk about the condition of the country that at no other time were conditions in any other country comparable to what we have in Canada to-day. Let me call your attention to what this writer says. Speaking of the conditions, that existed in Great Britain during the Napoleonic wars, he says:
For the last twenty years England had been the only country in western Europe free from the devastating effects of military operations. She had consequently been called upon 'to supply the commercial needs of the whole world, and, thanks to the recent improvements in agriculture and in manufacturing industry, she was in a position to do so. The result was seen in a totally unprecedented expansion of foreign trade.
The conditions with us during the war while our sons were fighting overseas were the same as when the sons of Britain were fighting one hundred years ago on the Continent. We were freed from the devastating influence of the war itself, and we had an unprecedented period of prosperity in this country, a period of unusual development of our agricultural and industrial life, with the greatest foreign trade we ever had since confederation. But what was the reaction that came in England? This writer says that almost immediately after the war:
Bad harvests and violent fluctuations of prices were bringing widespread ruin upon agriculturalists. In the hope of assisting them the legislature in 1815 prohibited the importation of wheat until the price reached 80 s. a quarter. But this afforded no relief when, as in 1816, the price fell to 52s. 6d. It is easy to blame farmers for their folly in taking leases' at rents calculated upon war prices, and to condemn landlords for extortion.
Just as it is easy to say that the people took on too much land in the West:
But meanwhile the course of English industries appeared to be threatened with imminent ruin. Reports received by the Board of Agriculture in response to a circular letter issued in 1816 attest the severity of the crisis. Farmers, who a few years ago were competing eagerly for farms, were sending in notices to
Supply-Immigration

quit, and many farms were unlet; mortgagees found it difficult to realize; credit was collapsing; banks were failing in all directions; substantial farmers were becoming parish paupers. And while the producer was ruined the consumer derived no benefit. In December, 1816, wheat which in the spring had fallen to 52s. 6d. rose to 103s. Agriculture had become a mere gamble.
The condition was even worse in England than that portrayed by the hon. member for Bow River last night. It continued:
If landlords and farmers were ruined, merchants and manufacturers were in no better plight. . . . Traders, as is their wont, looked no further than their noses. The inevitable happened. With the restoration of normal conditions the continental demand for English goods rapidly slackened; prices came down with a run; production was paralysed, and thousands of hands wen turned adrift to swell the army of the unemployed. . .
As William Cobbett himself observed: "When men are in distress they are out of humour: they have not time and are not in a disposition to listen to reason." .... Because work was scarce, machinery was smashed and factories were destroyed. . . . Nor was the unrest confined to the agricultural counties. The Tyneside colliers, the Preston cotton-weavers, the Wiltshire cloth-workers, the Monmouthshire and Staffordshire ironworkers, the jute-workers of Dundee,-all alike were in ferment, demanding more employment, higher wages, and cheaper food.
That was the condition of affairs which faced the statesmen of the Mother Country-after the Napoleonic wars. The picture portrayed there was a very grave and a very dark one indeed. We have'no such dark picture confronting us in this country to-day. We had a period of unprecedented prosperity and of high prices during the war. Then the reaction came and prices fell. Conditions have not been righted, and that is one of the reasons why this discussion has been brought on. But here in this marvellous land of ours, with a territory exceeding that of the United States with great undeveloped mineral wealth as well as great tracts of agricultural lands that have not been opened up, with our great forests, our fisheries and all the other resources in this land which could support a population of 100,000,000 as well as the population of 8,000,000 that we have to-day, are we going to sit down helplessly and hopelessly and say that we do not expect to see the conditions arise under which all that we might hope for would come? I had the honour and distinction of coming to this parliament some twenty years ago and of imbibing from that great statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, some of that inspiration and belief in the future of this country which dominated him in his long political career. He told us and told the Canadian people twenty years ago of his abiding faith that the twentieth century would be .Canada's century, and I am satisfied that out of the mist and gloom and uncertainty of these days, which while it exists to-day is not at all comparable to what is to be found

among other nations of the world, if we but-play our part properly in the days that are to come, that prophetic utterance of his will be fulfilled.
Let us also look at the situation in the United States at the time of the Civil War. There was a great nation absolutely rent asunder by an internecine struggle between the North and the South. Immediately following the war came a period of depression. Their currency became degraded, and that country might almost have been looked upon in the view of the world outside as a nation with no hope for the future. Yet with that wonderful spirit of unity and the development of a national spirit which came to the United States of America, they entered upon a period of prosperity and advancement which in the next fifty years made them the greatest nation in the history of the world. And so we have lessons to learn from the experience of the Mother Country one hundred years ago, and lessons to learn from the experience of the great people to the south of us sixty years ago, and shall we not stop for a moment and see whether the paths they have trod, the lines which they have laid down, and which resulted in their advancement and progress and prosperity, are not such as we might also well follow?
One of the great things we lack in this country to-day is a national spirit. If there is any one thing the Canadian people need, and to this task no matter to which party we may owe allegiance to-day we might well join together and devote ourselves, it is the development of the idea of a great Canada whose sons we ought all to be proud to be; it is the realization that has come to us in this generation carrying on from the generations that have gone before in this wonderful land with its free institutions, where no man is discriminated against on account of birth, religion or station, where the highest position in the gift of the people is open to the man of honesty, ability and integrity, as we have had the fact recorded in this very debate by the hon. member for Springfield who so eloquently told the story of our possibilities. In order that we may develop that spirit, we must see to it that sectionalism is eliminated in this country. Instead of this continual argument going on about the attitude of antagonism between the man in the workshop and the man on the farm, let us realize that in this House, I venture to say, the greater percentage are farmers or sons of farmers, men born on the farm who have occupied prominent judicial and business positions and a high status both in this parliament and elsewhere in this

and other countries. Why should there be any antagonism between the different classes in this country? Rather than that there should be any antagonism between the men in the workshops and mines and the men on the farms, let us vie with each other to be co-mates and partners in everything that makes for the progress and advancement of this our common country.
How can the hon. member prevent the development of antagonism between classes if there is a feeling that one class is exploiting another?

If certain gentlemen	like my hon.	friend for
Brant (Mr. Good) wish to preach the gospel of class consciousness in this country they are doing little	to promote
the development of national spirit. I do not believe, Sir, that in this country there is any occasion to preach such a gospel. If there ever was a country that is free from any social condition in which you have upper classes, or middle classes, or lower classes that country is Canada. In that respect we are far in advance of our friends in the United States who, in their hundred years or so of history, have developed an aristocratic class-a class aristocratic as to wealth-which, in its disregard to the rights of the people, is far different even from the aristocracy of birth which exists in the Old Country. But here, in this free land, where the men of to-day are the successors of the workers of yesterday, and where the reward always comes to integrity, to effort, and to industry, we have a condition where there is no room for the existence of class consciousness, no matter in what quarter it is advocated.

I object to the hon. member insinuating that I was preaching, and have preached, class consciousness. I asked him a straight question as to how we were to prevent the development of these antagonisms if there was a feeling among these classes that injustice had been wrought.

I admit it.

Just as there are selfish men in office too, but the selfiish men in any of these occupations are not the men to take the lead in influencing thought in this country but rather men of greater breadth of view.

Can my hon. friend point out an instance in the history of British political life, or economic life, wherein the solution of the difficulty was not attended by the presence of class consciousness, I refer particularly to the problems that arose after the Napoleonic wars? '

ties that the hon. gentlemen opposite complain of would not have existed to-day, or if they did exist would have disappeared, had the view not been entertained then by a great many that for all time the trade of Canada must flow east and west; had we realized that we cannot be a hermit nation but must trade with our neighbors, and with other nations. However, there is no use in arguing that a movement towards class consciousness is going to remedy a trade condition. We have got to realize this, that in all parts of Canada we are suffering from the after effects of the war, from the deflation which is going on-following an abnormal prosperity and development that occurred during the four years of that great struggle. We must all pull together in Canada and apply ourselves resolutely to the problems which confront us so that we may be able to pass on to those who come after us a prosperous land and a happy condition of affairs as the result of our administration and our efforts.
We are told that men are leaving the farms and going to the cities. Well, they have been leaving the farms and going to the cities during all the ages. They have been going also to the United States; they have been going to and from the United States for a great many years. In eastern Canada, comparing the conditions which exist to-day with those which prevailed when I first had the honour of a seat in the Nova Scotia legislature, I remember the time when the young men of our province used to take their axes, go into the forest, hew down the trees, and make homes for themselves. They do not do that to-day. There came the lure of the free lands of the West. Harvest excursions were introduced, the boys of the East were carried out west there to learn that they could acquire 160 acres of land by simply staying on that land six months a year for two years. They went out to the West, saw the land which did not need the axe in order to bring it into a state suitable for cultivation, and thousands of them settled there. To-day the men in the East are not willing to go out and cut down the forest to make homes for themselves as their predecessors used to do with this exception: that the sons of Quebec still retain the wonderful pioneering instinct of the men who settled on the banks of the St. Lawrence two or three centuries ago, in greater degree than people in other portions of Canada. Our people have felt the lure of the cities, they have experienced the stirring of life that the twentieth century has brought with it, they have

felt the development of materialism that has been going on not only in the cities but also among the tillers of the soil. The present situation is, perhaps, not due to any financial or economic reason; it is due to inherent conditions which have prevailed at all times but have become more deeply -accentuated within the last few years. We see the same thing in the United States. I read with interest a speech made in New York by Judge Manton, a distinguished jurist, who declared that the United States had lost by emigration during the last calendar year 100,000 of its workers-men who had come from southern Europe, had tarried for a period, and had gone home. The country, in the meantime, had received 32,000 people who had come to take the place of the 100,000 workers referred to. What was the situation last fall over there? Plans were drawn for the construction of public and other buildings to the extent of over five billions of dollars. Then the call came to the worker in Canada and every other worker elsewhere who was out of employment. Do we forget one of the difficulties we have in this country that when the snow comes in November there is a period of six months when our workers cannot engage in any outside employment? Thousands of these men have gone over there temporarily. They have gone from my province. They went from the city of Halifax which was partially destroyed during the war by an explosion. After that explosion men came from all parts of the Maritime provinces to engage in the work of reconstruction. When that was finished they went to the United States, to engage in this wonderful building movement which developed there. They are gone, but they are coming back again, and I say there is no reason why we should be fainthearted on account of either of these things. In the cycle of events all these problems come and go, but if we have abiding faith in the possibilities of Canada, then let us look forward with confidence to the future.

When the
committee rose at six o'clock, I was endeavouring to deal with that phase of the discussion which was referred to by several hon. gentlemen as to the fact that there was a continual flow of emigration from Canada to the United States. Some hon. gentlemen went so far as to argue that, therefore, we should take no steps for further immigration to this country. I was pointing out the unique situation that that great country to the south occupies, the fact that for a great number of years there was a continual flow back and forth between the two countries, and the further fact that last autumn there developed in the United States a tremendous boom involving an expenditure running into billions of dollars. This naturally drew from Canada, in the autumn and winter months, men who were unable to engage in outside work in this country. In addition to that, in considering this question, we must always remember that we are situated alongside a country with a population of a hundred million people, with wonderful diversity of climate, which enables the people within its borders to engage, at all seasons of the year, in vocations to which they are accustomed. Another fact in this connection that we must not forget, is that the United States, of all nations which participated in the war, came through in the best financial position. Almost every European country is debtor to the United States, and she succeeded in obtaining and in bringing within her borders the greatest percentage of the available gold in the world. That has been her situation. Therefore, she was better able than other countries in which these advantages did not exist, to stand the reaction which followed the war, and she had the further advantage, owing to the fact that she did not enter the war until a later date, of having participated probably to a greater extent than any other country, in the benefits resulting from the tremendous expenditure, on supplies required during the war. So that it was natural that, during that period, those who might, for the time being, be out of employment in Canada, might find their way to the United States.
It is also well worth remarking that the United States was the one great democratic country that, during the war, did not find it necessary to destroy its party alignment in order to carry on its affairs. The historic Republican and Democratic parties maintained their identity and worked together through all the problems that came before that great nation. I am sure the lesson which we ought to learn from the magnificent position she occupies to-day, should not be lost upon, some hon. gentlemen in this House.

The fact is so self-evident that it is hardly necessary to give an explanation. In Canada, ever since the war, we have been under the shadow of the swing of the pendulum that occurred after the tremendous prosperity that existed in this country, the high prices that were paid for and received from agricultural products, the continued activity of our industries in the East, all this creating an abnormal condition which naturally was followed by the situation which we have before us. Fortunately, we are beginning to see the turn of the road. Last year's great crops in the Northwest helped to bring back the nation's poise once more; and as we are awaiting the advent of spring, from all parts of Canada, from the eastern provinces as well as from far-off British Columbia, comes the word: The Canadian people are looking forward with confidence and hope to a renewal of normal conditions under which this country made such marvellous progress in the twenty years before the war. Under those conditions we have no reason to doubt the fact that we should look for, maintain and support a vigorous and aggressive policy of immigration. I take it that notwithstanding the remarks we have heard as to the lack of necessity for attempting to obtain immigration into this country, hon. gentlemen will agree that we are the one great undeveloped country of the northern zone whose resources have yet been touched only in the slightest degree, and that the need is apparent for more people to develop the available wealth of this country. Perhaps, I have been labouring that argument, because I am sure hon. gentlemen will agree as to the necessity of activity along those lines having regard to the problems before the people, and the advantage and necessity of having additional population to cope with them.
What is the class of people that we should have in this country? We have had various arguments and suggestions in regard to that. I was interested in seeing what Abraham Lincoln, whose language and whose predictions have almost come to be regarded as the voice of a seer, said in one of his wonderful utterances as to the conditions that existed and should exist in the country to the south of us. He said:
We should welcome every person of good family who really means to incorporate himself into our society, but repel all who will not be a real addition to the health and strength of the United States.
It seems to me that that general statement is one we might well adopt with regard to the immigrants who come here. I believe there should be no restriction as to nationality or religion with respect to the men who are

to come to Canada. The test as laid down by Lincoln is one. that I think we might well apply to everyone who' comes here to participate in our Canadian citizenship and take part in building up this country. We do not want any laggards in this country, but men and women who are industrious, and who realize that indolence and indifference will lead to failure here as in any other country.
Hon. gentlemen who come from other parts of Canada have spoken of the advantages of their own particular part of the country, and in that connection reference has been made particularly to the West. I am free to say that I think those of us who come from the Maritime provinces have been altogether too modest in asserting the advantages which would flow to the immigrant who should settle in our part of the country. We cannot boast of wheat fields that will yield the products of the earth simply by a little scratching, and by that I mean that fertilization is required, but we can boast of this, that the settler who comes to our part of Canada will be able to find a home there, not necessarily in the forest, but close by the forest, where he can get his wood to keep his family and himself warm, and where he has no difficulty in getting water for his household and his stock. There he will be beside the great ocean which yields with the slightest possible effort the best food any settler could have in the fish that swim in the sea. We have also there rich fruit belts, and the conditions as to living and the social conditions generally offer to anyone with a limited capital, even the settler who com^ to Canada with only $2,000 as; his entire capital an opportunity to make a home for himself and his family in the provinces down by the sea under better conditions I believe than obtain in any other part of Canada. When he has started his home there, he will be able to live with less effort than he would elsewhere, because nature has so generously endowed that part of the country with those things that the poor but able and industrious man looks for in the place where he wants to make his home. That is the place I think where these immigrahts who come to our shores should settle.
There are many problems that have been suggested in connection with this question. I do not profess to be an expert upon it. I believe that the question of the best regulation of immigration is a very difficult and a very important one, and personally I would be disposed to leave in a very broad way to the minister, who has given very careful attention to this subject, the solution of these various problems.

We hear a great deal about the British Empire colonization scheme. It is a singular thing that for the first time in the history of the Empire, Great Britain has embarked upon the policy of assisted emigration. Never before-has she undertaken to engage in the policy of assisting her people to go abroad, either to other parts of the Empire or elsewhere. The necessity for this action has been unquestionably due to the tremendous amount the unemployment doles have reached. I do not mean to say that that is the sole reason why the proposition is made that Great Britain should help send her people to all parts of our far-flung Empire and participate in their upbuilding, but still that fact does exist, and a proposition is made which would involve the assumption by Canada of very grave and very serious obligations if she undertakes to participate in the scheme. It does seem to me that there are a great many problems involved in questions of this kind, and the solution of this immigration problem is one in which the self-reliance and th< energy of the individual immigrant ought to be trusted to a very great degree if it is going to result successfully.
I view with some alarm the proposition that we should bring'people out wholesale to this country, find land for them, pay them to stay on the land, and altogether finance them. Why, if Canadians are ever to be worth while, the men of to-day must do like our fathers did, and go out relying on themselves to build their homes and establish themselves in this country. It has become the fashion to-day to ask the government to have a finger in every pie, and if every man who is to come to this country is to be financed from the general treasury, that is a proposition that must be very seriously considered. I welcome as I am sure every Canadian should welcome, as many people from the Old Country as can come here, for naturally we would like to have them join with us in the development of Canada and the upbuilding of the Empire, but I think this matter should be approached with the greatest possible care. I do not wish to be understood as absolutely condemning it, but I think the minister should give it the gravest consideration and the closest possible attention in order that the correct solution of the problem may be arrived at. I think that with a return of prosperity to this country, which I believe is coming, we car safely leave the selection to the man who desires to get away from the difficult conditions in Europe and elsewhere, and who is looking abroad for an opportunity to make a new home for himself and family, and with all the 79 i
advantages Canada has to offer, I think that with the advent of prosperity this country will prove a great attraction to- these men fron across the sea.
With reference to the Canada Colonization scheme, I gathered from the statement made by the minister the other day that we di< not have before us the full facts in the matter, and personally I propose to await with interest the fuller statement which we were promised later on in this debate. In this connection let me remind hon. gentlemen that though some severe criticisms have been made, we have also had tributes paid to the immigration law of this country as it stands to-day. Judge Manton, federal judge for the state of New York, and one of the leading jurists of the United States, in discussing about a month ago what he regarded as the inequalities and injustices of the American law went on to point out this:
Our younger neighbor at the north, Canada, can teach us a lesson in dealing with the question of immigration. Its law is simple and direct. There the immigration officer may admit any immigrant who otherwise complies with the provisions of the immigration act, if it is shown to his satisfaction that such immigrant is (a) a bona fide agriculturalist entering Canada to farm, with sufficient means to begin farming in Canada; (b) a bona fide farm labourer to follow that occupation, who has reasonable assurance of employment; (c) a female domestic servant with reasonable assurance of employment, or any other labourer who has reasonable assurance of employment.
The. wife and family are admitted with the immigrant labourer. The passport must be vised by Canadian immigration officers stationed in Canada and simple provisions are made which aid and invite the immigrant to the shores of Canada.
Notwithstanding the criticisms that have been made of our immigration system, this statement made by a gentleman who is unquestionably an expert and has studied all the phases of the American immigration problem is an indication that we are quite up-to-date in the immigration law we have in this country.
I have detained this committee at very much greater length than I intended. I merely wish to say in conclusion that I hope every man who takes part in this discussion will feel, when expressing his views on this problem of immigration, that we are dealing, or ought to deal, with it in the most serious manner, entirely apart from any local or any narrow political consideration, and animated solely by the greatest possible faith in the future of our common country, and that we will do all we can to bring to this Dominion men and women who will come within Abraham Lincoln's estimate of what the citizens of a country ought to be. I hope that we will give to the government and the Acting

Mr. Chairman, the immigration question which is now before us is a national question. Nevertheless, it seems to me as though some hon. members have been looking at it from a merely local viewpoint. My sympathies to-day are with the Acting Minister of Immigration in his, efforts to solve this great problem in the interests of Canada. I believe the government need constructive criticism of their policy, and I will try to offer to-night suggestion-3 "'hich may be helpful.
Economic conditions in Canada to-day, as previous speakers have said are poorly balanced, and are mainly attributable to the war, but local factors and conditions have also had their influence. It is a trait of human nature to try and pass the blame on to someone else when things go wrong, but I think if we are courageous we will take our share of the blame and admit that we have contributed in some degree to the position in which we find ourselves at present.
I contend that many of the farmers who are in great difficulty-and that such is the case cannot be denied-are responsible to some extent for the existing trouble. I do not wish to underestimate the picture painted by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland)-he was conscientious in expressing his views, and I give him credit for it but I do not think that conditions are as bad as described even over the entire West. The farmers, in my opinion, helped to a certain extent to bring about the difficulties from which we are now suffering. During the war years they allowed their judgment, to some extent, to be warped. They got out of alignment with the true conditions and in good years did not conduct their operations wisely. They were not sufficiently careful in their expenditures during the period of high prices and good crops. Following the big harvests of 1915 and 1916, we had five successive years of comparative crop failure in large areas covering thousands of square miles, with the result that in those areas there is great distress to-day. Hence, it is the duty of parliament to try and alleviate the condition of the people in those districts if it possibly can.
I also think that the labour unions-including the coal miners, the building trades, the

transportation workers, the railway and shipping interests-have all contributed towards making the problem as we find it to-day. The farmers have to sell their products on the open markets of the world in competition with cheap labour, and have to buy commodities produced at unionized prices. Our dollar, as one hon. member said, is to-day in reality only worth about seventy cents, while unionized produced goods are selling at prices in excess of their real value. Some of the farmers are afraid of over-production and the consequent reduction of the prices of the products which they sell. I do not like the idea of restricting production. I think it is a poor policy for any organization of people- whether it is producers of coal, or farm products, or anything else-to adopt. Restricting production in an effort to make high prices only creates poverty. The world does not need high prices for anything; high prices denote a scarcity in some quarter. An extremely high price for wheat would be reasonable evidence that there was a famine in some country. Surely we do not want a condition of that kind. I think that what we are suffering from very largely is underconsumption. Most of us realize that Europe is our main market for food products to-day, and Europe is in a chaotic condition. The great mass of people there are not eating as they would if they were working steadily. Consequently they cannot buy, and we cannot sell our products. This big problem cannot be righted in a day; its solution is going to take time even though we all do our utmost, and even though a greater degree of harmony prevails in the future than in the past among European governments.
I would like to see greater production in every line of activity, in every line of industry. To-day we have a big overhead expense in running this country. We have railways which would carry several times as much freight as they are carrying to-day; we have a post office system large enough to cater to the needs of twenty-five or thirty millions of people. But our overhead has to be met, even though we have but a comparatively small population, just as much as though our population were far in excess of what it is. I think, therefore, it behooves us to get people into Canada in order to utilize those public facilities which are costing us so much, and thus help to lighten the per capita burden. To-day we have great natural wealth which is lying undeveloped. Natural wealth in its raw state is more of a liability than an asset if it is not worked. I think that what Canada needs is the intelligent application of labour to our natural resources so as to de-

velop and work them up to nearer 100 per cent of capacity. When Canada reaches that stage many of the economic difficulties from which we now suffer will have disappeared.
I would give prospective settlers, as nearly as possible, the actual facts about Canada. I would not try to picture the prospects for settlers in colours too rosy. Let the actual facts be stated, and if the truth will not attract settlers let them stay away. A dissatisfied settler will do more harm to the immigration policy of Canada than anything else. If we can succeed in satisfying settlers that will be the best immigration agency we could have. Hard conditions are not confined to Canada; they obtain in many other countries including the great United States. I will not admit that conditions are roseate throughout the entire republic, although that is what we have been hearing so much about to-day. In some of the great middle western states farming is in a precarious condition to-day, due to an over-inflation of the price of land when the war was on. In the great states of Iowa and Illinois, where the price of land went up to three or four hundred dollars an acre, they were fortunate enough during the war to get big crops, and, as we all know, they got tremendous prices. That threw the farmers generally off the track, and they overvalued their lands. Farm lands were sold for three or four hundred dollars an acre. Many farmers sold their small holdings and bought larger ones. The result is that thousands of those farmers are absolutely bankrupt and are looking for new places to locate and start in business. These farmers would make the very best settlers that Canada could procure.
I am sorry, for this reason, that the member for Bow River painted as blue a picture as he did, because the American agents will use the statements that have been made on the floor of this House to try and keep people from coming to Canada. I know that the United States government had two men in the city of Regina before I came down here, trying to get settlers to go to the States. They were working among the Mennonites, trying to show them they could give them better terms in the States than they were getting here. A friend of mine in western Canada, an exAmerican farmer, told me shortly before Christmas that a neighbour of his who was very much dissatisfied with conditions in Alberta, took his boys and went back to their old stamping ground in the States. They found conditions even worse there than in northern Alberta when they left. They returned to northern Alberta.
There are many people in England, Ireland and Scotland who would improve their positions very much if they came to Canada. The same is true of the Scandinavian countries, and Germany, Holland, Denmark and Switzerland. Large numbers of the people in these countries would be delighted to come to Canada. I do not like to mention matters that come under my personal notice, but I will give one instance which will give the House a little idea of what can be done. A neighbour of mine, a German farmer, got his sister-in-law and six children to come out here. They have been here about 17 months. Shortly before I left home he came to my house and told me that it cost SI,600 to bring that family out here-a widow with her six children, the youngest being eight years old and the eldest a girl of twenty. In fifteen months they had paid back the $1,600 and had $300 in the bank. That man said the family were simply delighted with everything in Canada, it was so much better than conditions in Germany. Those people make the very best settlers Canada can get. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we should forget about the alien enemy and try to do the right thing by these people. The great common masses of Germany are not the people who brought on the war. It was the military element that was in the saddle and forced the situation, but the great common people were not to blame for it any more than our working classes were to blame. I would like to see the restrictions against alien enemy countries lifted, and would like to see all good, sane, worthy people brought in. We want everybody who is willing to take off his coat and go to work and who would not be too particular about what work he did. These people would be valuable citizens in Canada. It used to be said that every man was estimated by the government as being worth $1,000 to the country. The greatest asset Canada can have is her people, and I submit that those people make settlers that are second to none. They are not afraid to encounter hardships, and we may as well admit that settlers have to suffer hardships. It is not a bed of roses and we should not hold up such a picture before prospective settlers, because if we do we will only have dissatisfied settlers, who will go some place else, and we will have spent our money in vain.
Referring to the conditions under which new settlers should expect to start in this country, some people expect they are coming to a ready-made farm. I do not think it is at all necessary to give them that idea. Canada
